readings.position: Diekamp calls Halloix's book a 'krasse Tendenzschrift' (crass special pleading) whose aim was to clear Origen of every suspicion. He records that Cave, Dupin, Lequien and Walch nonetheless thought Halloix's explanation 'essentially justified, or at least probable'.

readings.work: History of the Christian Church, vol. III (rev. 1884), §144
readings.position: In canon 11 'the connection is incongruous', and the name 'is regarded by Halloix, Garnier, Jacob Basnage, Walch, and others, as an interpolation. Noris and Hefele (ii. p. 874) maintain its genuineness.' Schaff himself leaves it open.

readings.work: History of the Councils IV (1895), p. 336, reprinted in NPNF II.14
readings.position: Hefele restates the argument (Origen was not among the heretics condemned by the first four councils, and does not belong with this group) and judges that it carries little weight.

passages.textual_notes: Halloix's own Latin was not reached; the Latin given is Garnier's report of his reasoning in §I ('Quid Halloixius nuper de quaestione senserit'), so it may paraphrase him. The transcription breaks off at 'intelligi s[…]'. 'Acephali' ('the headless') was a name for the anti-Chalcedonian party, who would have had no reason to leave Dioscorus in a list of heretics. OCR corrections in Diekamp: 'dienten' read as 'Clienten'. Where the eighteenth-century writers stood is reported inconsistently. Hefele and Schaff put 'Basnage' with Halloix. Diekamp puts Samuel Basnage with Baronius and Jacques (Jakob) Basnage with the mediating view (see the Diekamp passage below). The CCEL text of Schaff prints 'as all interpolation'; this is an obvious misprint for 'as an interpolation' and the quotation below is corrected. The chapter heading in PL 68 is 'CAPUT V. An damnatus sit reipsa Origenes in synodo V.', § I 'Quid Halloixius nuper de quaestione senserit' (col. 1073C), which matches the reference given. Diekamp notes a later revised version of Garnier's dissertation (in Hardouin's Theodoret Auctarium, Paris 1684); which version PL 68 reprints was not checked. Resolved on 2026-10-20: the sentence 'Deinde nemo non intelligit ...' stands inside Halloix's reasoning as Garnier reports it (it follows 'Sic igitur ratiocinatur'), so the four-councils argument is as old as 1648 in print. The page text still breaks off mid-word, so Garnier's own reply to it was not read.

passages.title: The early defenders of the condemnation: Baronius, Huet, Noris, the Ballerini
passages.author_work_ref: Franz Diekamp, Die origenistischen Streitigkeiten im sechsten Jahrhundert und das fünfte allgemeine Concil (1899), Einleitung
passages.original: Cäsar Baronius hielt dem Zustande der Synodalacten gegenüber das Zeugniß der alten Tradition für vollkommen ausreichend, um mit Sicherheit erweisen zu können, daß die fünfte allgemeine Synode Origenes und seine Lehren auf Grund besonderer Berathungen verurtheilt habe. Ihm schlössen sich, um nur einige hervorragende Vertreter dieser Ansicht zu nennen, mehr oder minder rückhaltlos Severinus Binius, Peter de Marca, Peter Daniel Huet, der Cardinal Heinrich Noris, Anton Pagi, Samuel Basnage, Claude Fleury, die Brüder Peter und Hieronymus Ballerini, Natalis Alexander, Remy Ceillier an.
passages.edition: F. Diekamp, Die origenistischen Streitigkeiten (Münster i. W.: Aschendorff, 1899), Einleitung, p. 2 (page approximate). The works it lists, as Diekamp cites them: P. D. Huet, Origeniana (Rouen, 1668); H. Noris, Dissertatio historica de Synodo quinta (Padua, 1673, with the Historia Pelagiana); P. and H. Ballerini, Defensio dissertationis Norisianae de Synodo V. adversus dissertationem P. Garnerii, in Noris, Opera omnia IV (Verona, 1732).
passages.checked_against: archive.org scan of the 1899 printing (OCR text), item dieorigenistisch00diek.
passages.english: Caesar Baronius held that, given the state of the synodal Acts, the testimony of the ancient tradition was quite sufficient to prove with certainty that the fifth general synod had condemned Origen and his teachings after separate deliberations. To name only a few eminent representatives of this view, he was followed, more or less without reserve, by Severinus Binius, Pierre de Marca, Pierre-Daniel Huet, Cardinal Enrico Noris, Antoine Pagi, Samuel Basnage, Claude Fleury, the brothers Pietro and Girolamo Ballerini, Natalis Alexander and Remy Ceillier.
passages.why_it_matters: It shows the opposing camp, which held that the council itself condemned Origen. Its main argument was what ancient readers said happened, not the state of the Acts.

readings.work: Dissertatio historica de Synodo quinta (1673), as summarised in NPNF II.14, Excursus on the XV Anathemas
readings.position: Origen 'was twice condemned by the Fifth Synod': once on his own before the eight sessions whose Acts survive, and again after them together with Didymus the Blind and Evagrius.

readings.work: Defensio dissertationis Norisianae de Syn. V. adv. diss. P. Garnerii (1732), as summarised in NPNF II.14
readings.position: They defended Noris against Garnier and 'expand and amend Noris's hypothesis'.

readings.work: Origeniana (Rouen, 1668), as classified by Diekamp (1899)
readings.position: Diekamp lists Huet among those who followed Baronius. Huet's own words on the fifth council were not found. Huet's Origeniana is a well-known sympathetic study of Origen (general knowledge, not checked here).

readings.work: As quoted in NPNF II.14, Excursus (Diekamp cites Lehrbuch der Dogmengeschichte II³, 1894, p. 396 for Harnack's view)
readings.position: Harnack says in a footnote that he agrees with 'Noris, the Ballerini, Möller ... and Loofs ... as against Hefele and Vincenzi'. Writing of the Fifth Council he says, 'It condemned Origen, as Justinian desired; it condemned the Three Chapters and consequently the Antiochene theology, as Justinian desired'.

readings.work: Ecclesiastical History IV.38, trans. E. Walford (1846)
readings.position: The synod wrote back to Justinian 'after they had uttered exclamations against Origen', and Evagrius quotes it binding such a one 'in the cords of our anathema'. This is the tradition Baronius relied on.

readings.scholar: Pierre Halloix (as reported by Franz Diekamp)
readings.work: Diekamp, Die origenistischen Streitigkeiten (1899), Einleitung, pp. 2–3 (page approximate)
readings.position: Halloix, wishing to clear Origen of every suspicion, 'denied any condemnation of his client at the fifth general synod' and held the two passages in the fifth and eighth sessions to be forgeries.
readings.side: council did not condemn Origen; passages forged

passages.textual_notes: OCR corrections made: '(lüs;ir' read as 'Cäsar', 'hieli' as 'hielt', 'dafs' as 'daß'. The camp held more than that the name in canon 11 was genuine. Its claim was that the council discussed Origen separately, and that the Acts as we have them are incomplete. Hefele (below) gives up the separate trial and keeps the name. Diekamp's paragraph goes on to name nineteenth-century writers who share the view, among them Pusey, Möller, Loofs and Harnack (as summarised by the fetch tool; not read in full). Re-matching against the scan confirmed the German of the Baronius paragraph and the list of names word for word, apart from OCR noise.

passages.title: Vincenzi (1864–69): the fullest case for forgery
passages.author_work_ref: Aloysius (Luigi) Vincenzi, In S. Gregorii Nysseni et Origenis scripta et doctrinam nova recensio cum appendice de actis Synodi V. oecumenicae, as described by Diekamp (1899) and the NPNF editor (1900)
passages.original:
[Diekamp 1899:] In neuerer Zeit steht Aloisi Vincenzi mit ganzer Seele auf Halloix' Seite, ja er geht in seinem immerfort und überall Mißverständnisse, absichtliche Verdrehungen und böswillige Fälschungen witternden Werke noch über diesen hinaus, insofern er auch Justinians Edict gegen Origenes für unecht erklärt und es für ein dem Kaiser nur überreichtes, in Syrien entstandenes Actenstück ausgibt.
[NPNF II.14, 1900:] It would seem that this cannot possibly refer to anything else than a condemnation of Origen by the Fifth Ecumenical Synod, and so strongly is Vincenzi, Origen's defender, impressed with this that he declares the passage to have been tampered with.
passages.edition: L. Vincenzi, In S. Gregorii Nysseni et Origenis scripta et doctrinam nova recensio cum appendice de actis Synodi V. oecumenicae (Rome: Bernardi Morini, 1864–69); Diekamp cites vol. IV (1865) and vol. V (1869), appendix II. Pages not confirmed. Diekamp, Die origenistischen Streitigkeiten (1899), Einleitung, pp. 3–4 (page approximate). NPNF II.14, Excursus on the XV Anathemas against Origen.
passages.checked_against: Diekamp: archive.org scan (OCR). NPNF: CCEL. Vincenzi's own volumes were not opened; Google Play confirms the title and the 1864 printer.
passages.english:
[Diekamp:] In recent times Aloisi Vincenzi stands wholeheartedly on Halloix's side. Indeed, in his work, which scents misunderstandings, deliberate distortions and malicious forgeries everywhere and at every turn, he goes further still: he declares even Justinian's edict against Origen spurious, and passes it off as a document drawn up in Syria and merely presented to the emperor.
[NPNF: English original as above.]
passages.english_source: Diekamp: own translation. NPNF: public domain English.
passages.why_it_matters: Vincenzi is the main nineteenth-century source of the interpolation case, and Hefele answers him among others in his note on canon 11. He went further than anyone: he threw out not only the name and the Session V passage but Justinian's 543 edict as well.

readings.work: Nova recensio … cum appendice de actis Synodi V. oecumenicae (1864–69), as reported by Hefele, Diekamp and the NPNF editor
readings.position: Origen's name in canon 11 is a later insertion, the Session V reference to Origen has been tampered with, and Justinian's edict against Origen is not authentic. Harnack adds that he also sought to rehabilitate Vigilius.

readings.work: History of the Councils IV (1895), p. 336, reprinted in NPNF II.14
readings.position: Hefele says Vincenzi 'maintains with great zeal' that the name is a later insertion, and answers the arguments he and the others advance (see the Hefele passage).

readings.work: As quoted in NPNF II.14, Excursus on the XV Anathemas
readings.position: NPNF quotes Harnack calling 'this last author's book' (taken here to be Vincenzi's, which NPNF's sentence does not state) 'a big work which falsifies history to justify the theses of Halloix, to rehabilitate Origen and Vigilius, and on the other hand to "remodel" the Council and partly to bring it into contempt'.

readings.work: Die origenistischen Streitigkeiten (1899), Einleitung
readings.position: Diekamp presents Vincenzi as Halloix's heir, a writer who sees forgery everywhere. Diekamp's own reconstruction (see the Diekamp passage) treats the pre-conciliar anathemas as real.

passages.textual_notes: Title: the task brief and some modern summaries give 'nova defensio'. The title page (Google Play record) and Diekamp read 'nova recensio … cum appendice de actis Synodi V. oecumenicae'. Diekamp's OCR printed it as 'nova recensio'. OCR corrections in Diekamp: 'Jd neuerer Zeil' read as 'In neuerer Zeit', 'Vincen/i' as 'Vincenzi', 'Edictgegen' as 'Edict gegen'. The status V applies to the reports by Diekamp and NPNF, which were read. Vincenzi's own Latin was not reached.

passages.title: Hefele's verdict ('mere conjecture') and the NPNF editor's ('no possible reason to doubt')
passages.author_work_ref: K. J. von Hefele, A History of the Councils of the Church IV (Eng. trans. 1895), p. 336, note on canon XI of 553, reprinted in NPNF II.14; H. R. Percival, NPNF II.14, Excursus on the XV Anathemas (1900)
passages.language: English (W. R. Clark's 1895 translation of Hefele's German; Percival wrote in English)
passages.original:
[Hefele:] Halloix, Garnier, Basnage, Walch and others suppose, and Vincenzi maintains with great zeal, that the name of Origen is a later insertion in this anathematism, because […] (c) because this anathematism is identical with the tenth in the omologia of the Emperor, […] but in the latter the name of Origen is lacking […] All these considerations seem to me of insufficient strength, or mere conjecture, to make an alteration in the text and arbitrarily to remove the name of Origen. […] Finally, only on the ground that the name of Origen really stood in the eleventh anathematism, can we explain the widely-circulated ancient rumour that our Synod anathematized Origen and the Origenists.
[Percival:] That Origen was condemned by name in the Eleventh Canon of this council there seems no possible reason to doubt. But even if these anathemas were adopted at the Home Synod before the meeting of the Fifth Ecumenical, it is clear that by including his name among those of the heretics in the XIth Canon, it practically ratified and made its own the action of that Synod.
passages.edition: Hefele, Conciliengeschichte II, 2nd ed. (Freiburg, 1875); Diekamp cites pp. 790 ff., 859 ff., 898 f. for Hefele's treatment, and the exact page of this note in the German was not confirmed. English: A History of the Councils of the Church IV, trans. W. R. Clark (Edinburgh, 1895), p. 336 (as cited in NPNF). NPNF II.14 (New York, 1900). Schaff, History of the Christian Church III (rev. 1884), § 144, cites 'Hefele (ii. p. 874)' for the same view (edition of Hefele not stated).
passages.checked_against: NPNF II.14 as transcribed at tertullian.org and CCEL. The German original was not checked.
passages.why_it_matters: This is the classic answer to the interpolation case and the place most later writers quote. Hefele gives the four arguments for removing the name, then his replies and his three reasons for keeping it. Percival adds the point that matters most for the doctrinal debate: even if the fifteen anathemas came from an earlier synod, a genuine name in canon 11 adopts that synod's verdict.

readings.work: History of the Councils IV (1895), p. 336
readings.position: Hefele lists four arguments for removing the name: Ascidas the Origenist would have blocked it; only heretics condemned by the first four councils are listed; the emperor's homologia (confession of faith) omits Origen; Origen does not fit the group. He answers each. The emperor or the bishops may have gone beyond the homologia, and the Roman archive copy, the Palestinian Origenist monks' break with bishops who signed the Acts, and the ancient report of a condemnation all favour the name.

readings.work: NPNF II.14, Excursus on the XV Anathemas (1900)
readings.position: He sees 'no possible reason to doubt' the name. By naming Origen in canon 11 the council 'practically ratified' whatever earlier synod passed the anathemas. He also thinks Evagrius Scholasticus's testimony was set aside 'too peremptorily'.
readings.side: name genuine; council ratified the condemnation

readings.work: Die origenistischen Streitigkeiten (1899), Einleitung
readings.position: He describes Hefele's as the 'carefully grounded mediating view': no separate trial of Origen in 553, but a condemnation 'only in passing and in a heap' with the other heretics in canon 11.

readings.work: 'Did the Fifth Ecumenical Council Condemn Universal Salvation?', Eclectic Orthodoxy (31 May 2020)
readings.position: Kimel cites Hefele against the council's adoption of the fifteen anathemas ('It is by no means probable … that this Fifth Ecumenical Council occupied itself with Origen in particular'). He does not take up Hefele's defence of the name, and accepts that the name stands in canon 11.

readings.work: 'Constantinople, 03: Second Council of (Fifth Ecumenical Council; 553 CE)', Brill Encyclopedia of Early Christianity Online (2019)
readings.position: Revives the points Hefele answered, the name's last and out-of-order place and its absence from the earlier list in Justinian's 'Homonoia', and concludes 'This suggests an interpolation.' The entry does not discuss Hefele's replies.

passages.textual_notes: The NPNF transcription at CCEL prints 'new Lama' for 'New Lavra' (the Palestinian monastery). One web transcription of the same page appeared to the fetch tool to read 'scent to me' for 'seem to me'; the CCEL text reads 'seem', which is adopted. The bracketed ellipses in the quotation mark where text was skipped; the wording of reason (c) was matched only in substance, not word for word. 'Omologia' is Hefele's transliteration of ὁμολογία ('confession'), meaning Justinian's 551 confession of faith on the Three Chapters, whose tenth anathema Hefele and Crouzel compare with canon 11. The sources do not agree on what 'Homonoia' names (see other findings). Hefele's 'widely-circulated ancient rumour' is not itemised in the part of the note read; the ancient witnesses usually cited for it are Cyril of Scythopolis, Evagrius Scholasticus and the later councils. Checked again on 2026-10-20 at tertullian.org: the note is headed 'Notes.' and cites Hist. Councils, Vol. iv., p. 336; it prints 'the monks of the new Lama in Palestine', evidently a misprint for Lavra.

passages.title: Diekamp (1899): the mediating view and the new reconstruction
passages.author_work_ref: Franz Diekamp, Die origenistischen Streitigkeiten im sechsten Jahrhundert und das fünfte allgemeine Concil (1899), Einleitung
passages.original: Weitaus die meisten Gelehrten unserer Tage treten der in der älteren Zeit durch Heinrich Valesius und Jakob Basnage aufgestellten, neuerdings durch Carl Joseph v. Hefele sorgfältig begründeten vermittelnden Ansicht bei, daß besondere Synodalverhandlungen gegen Origenes nur auf der σύνοδος ἐνδημοῦσα zu Konstantinopel im Jahre 543 stattgefunden, daß aber auch das fünfte allgemeine Concil im Jahre 553 den Origenes und seine Irrthümer ausdrücklich, wenngleich „nur transeundo und in cumulo“ mit anderen Häretikern im elften Anathematismus verurtheilt habe. […] Wenn ich eine neue Behandlung der verwickelten und schwierigen Frage in Angriff zu nehmen wage, so geschieht es, weil ich glaube, daß eine von Grund auf neue Untersuchung der Quellen und insbesondere die Ausnutzung einiger bisher gar nicht verwertheter oder nicht ausreichend gewürdigter Documente uns der richtigen Lösung um ein Erhebliches näher zu bringen vermag.
passages.edition: F. Diekamp, Die origenistischen Streitigkeiten im sechsten Jahrhundert und das fünfte allgemeine Concil (Münster i. W., 1899), Einleitung, pp. 3–5 (page approximate).
passages.checked_against: archive.org scan of the 1899 printing (OCR). The scan text available to the tools stopped at about p. 31, so Diekamp's own later discussion of canon 11 was not read.
passages.english: By far the majority of scholars today hold the mediating view, put forward long ago by Henri de Valois and Jacques Basnage and recently grounded with care by Carl Joseph von Hefele. On this view separate synodal proceedings against Origen took place only at the resident synod (synodos endēmousa) at Constantinople in 543, but the fifth general council of 553 also condemned Origen and his errors expressly, if 'only in passing and in a heap' with other heretics, in the eleventh anathema. […] If I venture to take up this tangled and difficult question afresh, it is because I believe that a fundamentally new study of the sources, and in particular the use of some documents not used at all so far or not adequately weighed, can bring us considerably nearer to the right solution.
passages.why_it_matters: It records the state of the question in 1899: the interpolation thesis was by then a minority view, and Hefele's position, that the name is genuine, was the majority view among scholars. Diekamp then offered the reconstruction most historians still use, which places a real condemnation of Origenism by the same bishops just before the council opened. That reconstruction is about the fifteen anathemas; the step from there to the name's place in canon 11 is made by Price and Kimel, and was not read in Diekamp's own chapter.

readings.work: Die origenistischen Streitigkeiten (1899), as summarised by Grillmeier and Kimel
readings.position: Justinian had the bishops already gathered for the council deal with the Origenists before its formal opening on 5 May 553, and they passed the anathemas then (Kimel's account of Diekamp). Price and Kimel apply this to the name in canon 11; Diekamp's own chapter on canon 11 was not read.
readings.side: reconstruction of the fifteen anathemas (a pre-conciliar act); his treatment of the name in canon 11 not read

readings.work: As quoted by Kimel (2020); work and page not shown in the portion read
readings.position: The condemnation of the Origenists 'clearly belongs to the Council of 553, but cannot be placed after the opening of it'. It took place 'on the level of a synodus endemousa'.

readings.work: 'Origen and Origenism', Catholic Encyclopedia 11 (1911)
readings.position: 'Relying on the most recent studies' (that is, Diekamp), Prat holds that the Acts deal only with the Three Chapters, that only those Acts went to the pope, and that the anti-Origenist sentence was 'extra-conciliary' and later 'mistaken … for a decree of the actual ecumenical council'. He does not discuss the name in canon 11.

readings.work: Eclectic Orthodoxy (31 May 2020)
readings.position: Kimel reports that Diekamp's hypothesis 'has been embraced by most modern scholars and may now be considered the standard view'. He holds that Origen's name stands in canon 11, and in a later piece (2026) says that 'Origen is named without any specification of error'.

passages.textual_notes: OCR corrections made: 'ovvodog ivdrjfxovoa' read as 'σύνοδος ἐνδημοῦσα', 'Coli eil' as 'Concil', 'Irrthünier' as 'Irrthümer'. 'Synodos endēmousa' means the standing synod of bishops resident in the capital. 'Transeundo et in cumulo' means 'in passing and in a heap', and Diekamp puts it in quotation marks as Hefele's phrase. 'Heinrich Valesius' is Henri de Valois (1603–76), the editor of Evagrius Scholasticus.

passages.title: Crouzel: Origen missing from the emperor's speech and from Vigilius's letter
passages.author_work_ref: Henri Crouzel, 'Origen and Origenism', New Catholic Encyclopedia (as on Encyclopedia.com)
passages.original: Justinian opened the council without the agreement of Vigilius; and in its discussions little attention was paid to Origen, except to put his name in the list of heretics condemned in canon 11. He was not mentioned in the Emperor's opening discourse, which is the source of the council's anathemas, nor in the letter of Vigilius approving the council after the fact (Mansi 9:413–420). […] Following ordinary norms of interpretation, however, there is no question of holding that Origen was a formal heretic—the bishops were persuaded that he was a heretic through the belief of Epiphanius; nor is it necessary to admit that the errors with which he was charged are really his.
passages.edition: New Catholic Encyclopedia, article 'Origen and Origenism' (Origenism section signed H. Crouzel; subsection '6th Century'); edition, volume and page not confirmed (the Encyclopedia.com page gives no edition number). Vigilius's letter: Mansi IX, cols 413–420, as the article cites it.
passages.checked_against: Encyclopedia.com reproduction of the NCE article.
passages.english_source: In copyright; quoted briefly for discussion.
passages.why_it_matters: This is the clearest scholarly statement of the 'absence' arguments. Origen is not in Justinian's opening speech to the council, and not in the letter in which Vigilius later approved it. Crouzel uses them to limit what the name means. He does not use them to remove it.

readings.work: 'Les condamnations subies par Origène et sa doctrine', Origeniana Septima (1999), pp. 311–315, as translated by Alura (2021)
readings.position: In Alura's translation Crouzel notes that Origen's name is in canon 11 but that he is 'not found in the corresponding list' in Justinian's confession of faith (no. 10), and that he stands last though he is the oldest. He asks 'What is the sense of this addition?', suggests an allusion to earlier discussions, and answers 'No' to whether Origen should be considered canonically condemned by the Fifth Council, 'on account of what these canonical texts themselves say and their significant differences with his actual doctrines'.
readings.side: name present but anomalous; not canonically condemned

readings.work: Brill Encyclopedia of Early Christianity (2019)
readings.position: 'Vigilius' documents, emanated by a council that was not wanted by him, do not contain Origen's name.' Ramelli takes this as further evidence of interpolation.

readings.work: 'Responses to Father Kimel's Universalist Reblog', Orthodox Christian Theology (6 February 2021); the Price p. 43 citation is from 'Apocatastasis' Condemnation During the Council of Constantinople II' (17 November 2019)
readings.position: Expecting Origen in Justinian's 551 edict is 'anachronism', and 'We should not expect the constitutia [Vigilius's documents] to include Origen's name.' Truglia writes, 'I am aware of no known copy of the anathemas sent specifically to Vigilius preserved in the manuscript record.' In his 2019 article he quotes Price (vol. 1, p. 43) that 'In 543 Vigilius signed Justinian's edict condemning Origen'.

readings.work: Catholic Encyclopedia 11 (1911)
readings.position: 'Only the Acts concerning the affair of the Three Chapters were submitted to the pope for his approval, which was given on 8 December, 553, and 23 February, 554.' On this account Vigilius's silence about Origen is what one would expect.
readings.side: explains the papal silence without interpolation

readings.scholar: E. M. Harding (as summarised by Wikipedia)
readings.work: 'Origenist Crises', The Westminster Handbook to Origen (2004), p. 166, known only through Wikipedia
readings.position: Wikipedia's summary says Origen's name does not appear in 'the version of the conciliar proceedings that was eventually signed by Pope Vigillius, a long time afterwards'. That is a stronger claim than Crouzel's or Ramelli's, who say only that Vigilius's own approving documents do not contain the name. No manuscript or edition of the signed version is named.

passages.textual_notes: The Encyclopedia.com text matches the quotation word for word. It is Crouzel's own English in the New Catholic Encyclopedia and is not Alura's translation. Alura's translation is of Crouzel's 1999 French article (the reading below). The NCE text speaks of 'the Origenist monks of the 6th century', so a remark that 'Origenists of the fifth century' might be a slip does not apply to it; it belongs, if anywhere, to Alura's translation, where it was not re-checked. The 'opening discourse' is Justinian's letter read at Session I. Vigilius's approval came in his letter to Eutychius of 8 December 553 and his second Constitutum (a formal papal ruling) of 23 February 554 (dates from Prat 1911 and Wikipedia). The NPNF editor likewise notes that 'nothing whatever is said about Origen in the call of the council, nor in any of the letters written in connexion with it'.
passages.date: NCE article (date not confirmed); Crouzel's French article 1999

passages.title: Price (2009): the last place 'reflects the renewed condemnation' just before the council
passages.author_work_ref: Richard Price, The Acts of the Council of Constantinople of 553 with Related Texts on the Three Chapters Controversy (Translated Texts for Historians 51, Liverpool, 2009), vol. 2, p. 123 n. 86 (on canon 11), and vol. 1, p. 19 n. 40
passages.original:
[vol. 2, p. 123 n. 86, as quoted by Baghos:] reflects the renewed condemnation of Origenism by Justinian and the bishops immediately before the council formally opened.
[vol. 1, p. 19:] When discussing the anti-Origenist canons, I shall give the evidence that casts serious doubt on Ascidas' alleged Origenism.
passages.edition: R. Price (trans.), The Acts of the Council of Constantinople of 553 with Related Texts on the Three Chapters Controversy, Translated Texts for Historians 51, 2 vols (Liverpool University Press, 2009): vol. 2, p. 123, n. 86; vol. 1, p. 19, n. 40 (pointing to vol. 2, pp. 273–4).
passages.checked_against: vol. 1, p. 19: a PDF of the volume posted on Kimel's site (the text available to the tools ran only to p. 27). vol. 2, p. 123 n. 86: only as quoted by Mario Baghos, 'The Conflicting Portrayals of Origen in the Byzantine Tradition', Phronema 30.2 (2015), p. 73 and n. 10.
passages.why_it_matters: The council's English translator explains Origen's odd last place, one of the main internal arguments for interpolation, as the trace of a real and recent act. He also casts doubt on the oldest argument against the name: that Theodore Ascidas, an Origenist, would have stopped it.

readings.work: The Acts of the Council of Constantinople of 553 (2009), vol. 2, p. 123 n. 86, as quoted by Baghos (2015), p. 73 n. 10
readings.position: In the note Baghos quotes, Price says that the name's last place 'reflects the renewed condemnation of Origenism by Justinian and the bishops immediately before the council formally opened'. He takes the name as part of canon 11; no discussion of interpolation by Price was seen. Wikipedia, citing Price, adds that the bishops 'signed the canons condemning Origenism before the council formally opened'.
readings.side: name accepted; last place explained by a pre-conciliar act

readings.work: 'The Conflicting Portrayals of Origen in the Byzantine Tradition', Phronema 30.2 (2015), pp. 69–104, at p. 73
readings.position: He notes that the name 'appears last' and accepts Price's explanation. He does not say the name is interpolated.

readings.work: Comment of 27 December 2021, Shameless Orthodoxy
readings.position: 'I do not find the out-of-order argument compelling.' The last place 'simply testifies to the likelihood that the council fathers were appealing to a more recent condemnation of Origen'.

readings.work: Brill Encyclopedia of Early Christianity (2019)
readings.position: The same last place, 'notably out of chronological order', together with the missing name in Justinian's earlier list, 'suggests an interpolation'.

passages.textual_notes: Price's note on canon 11 was read only through Baghos's quotation; its full wording and context were not checked. Price's separate conjecture that the fifteen anathemas dropped out of the Latin Acts concerns those anathemas, not the name in canon 11.

passages.title: Today's exchange: Ramelli's case and McClymond's objection (2013–2019)
passages.author_work_ref: I. L. E. Ramelli, 'Constantinople, Second Council of', Brill Encyclopedia of Early Christianity (2019); M. McClymond, review in Theological Studies 76.4 (2015), p. 818 n. 10; Ramelli, 'Reply to Professor Michael McClymond', ibid., p. 832
passages.original:
[Ramelli 2019:] Only anathema 11 in the official acts mentions Origen, in the last position, and notably out of chronological order, in a list of heretics: […] In its sketch in Justinian's Homonoia (Concord), that list does not include the name of Origen. This suggests an interpolation. […] Vigilius' documents, emanated by a council that was not wanted by him, do not contain Origen's name.
[McClymond 2015:] If, as Ramelli suggests, the anathematizing of Origen—in the last place in Anathema 11—was not original, then the interpolation must have been added so quickly to the original text that no one recognized it as an interpolation. But then how is Ramelli—almost 1,500 years later—able to identify an interpolation when no one before her seems to have done so?
[Ramelli 2015:] Even setting aside that the interpolation was certainly not discovered by me, Photius in the ninth century could still read all of Origen's Peri Archōn in Greek […]
passages.edition: Ramelli, Brill Encyclopedia of Early Christianity Online (2019), DOI 10.1163/2589-7993_EECO_COM_040628. McClymond, 'Origenes Vindicatus vel Rufinus Redivivus?', Theological Studies 76.4 (2015), pp. 813–826, at p. 818 n. 10. Ramelli, 'Reply to Professor Michael McClymond', Theological Studies 76.4 (2015), pp. 827–835, at p. 832. Background: Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis (Leiden: Brill, 2013), p. 737 with n. 210 (as cited by McClymond).
passages.checked_against: The Brill entry as a PDF posted on Kimel's site; both Theological Studies PDFs on theologicalstudies.net.
passages.english_source: In copyright; quoted briefly for discussion.
passages.why_it_matters: This is the live academic form of the dispute. Ramelli gathers the internal arguments, and McClymond replies that a forgery nobody noticed for fifteen centuries is implausible. Ramelli answers that the interpolation was 'certainly not discovered by me'. She names no earlier proponent in that passage, but the case does go back to 1648.

readings.work: The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis (Leiden: Brill, 2013): 'is not the object of any authentic anathema' as quoted by Kimel (2020), no page given; 'was never formally condemned by any Christian ecumenical council' as quoted by McClymond (2015), p. 818 and p. 820, citing Ramelli p. 737 (with n. 210)
readings.position: Origen 'is not the object of any authentic anathema' (Kimel's quotation) and 'was never formally condemned by any Christian ecumenical council' (McClymond's quotation). These are her conclusions; McClymond treats them as resting on her view that the name in canon 11 is not original.

readings.work: Theological Studies 76.4 (2015), pp. 817–820
readings.position: Ramelli's claims of interpolation 'are designed to uphold Origen's reputation and minimize disagreements between Origen and other ancient Christian authors'. If the anathematizing of Origen in the last place in anathema 11 was not original, the interpolation must have been added so quickly that no one noticed, and he asks how she can see it 1,500 years later when 'no one before her seems to have done so'.

readings.work: 'Apokatastasis, Origen, and the Fifth Ecumenical Council (Part 3)', Eclectic Orthodoxy (9 January 2026), n. 33
readings.position: Origen's out-of-order place and the difference from the homonoia list have led historians 'over the past two hundred years' to wonder about interpolation. 'This minority view continues to find support among contemporary Church historians.' Kimel does not adopt it, and in 2021 rejected the out-of-order argument.
readings.side: reports interpolation as a respectable minority view

readings.work: 'Orthodoxy & Universal Salvation: Are the Two Compatible?', Shameless Orthodoxy (2021), comments of 26 January and 26 December 2021
readings.position: 'There is no smoking gun': no known manuscript lacks the name. Alura 'neither favor[s] nor disfavor[s]' interpolation and calls either opinion 'serious and respectable'.

readings.work: 'Origenist Crises', in J. A. McGuckin (ed.), The Westminster Handbook to Origen (2004), pp. 162–167, at p. 166, as summarised by Wikipedia
readings.position: In Wikipedia's wording, Origen's name 'does not appear at all in the Homonoia, the first draft of the anathemata issued by the imperial chancery', nor in the version of the proceedings later signed by Pope Vigilius. 'These discrepancies may indicate that Origen's name may have been retrospectively inserted into the text after the Council.'

passages.textual_notes: McClymond's 'no one before her seems to have done so' is mistaken as history: Halloix (1648), Garnier (1675), Walch and Vincenzi argued the same, as Hefele, Schaff and Diekamp record. His underlying point stands, though: no ancient or medieval reader is known to have suspected the name. In her reply (p. 832) Ramelli says only that the interpolation 'was certainly not discovered by me'; the passage names no earlier proponent. That the case goes back to 1648 comes from Hefele, Diekamp and Schaff, not from Ramelli's reply. Ramelli's 'Homonoia (Concord)' is probably, but not certainly, Justinian's 551 confession (ὁμολογία), which Hefele and Crouzel say has the matching list without Origen; Harding (via Wikipedia) calls the Homonoia 'the first draft of the anathemata issued by the imperial chancery', and Kimel (2026) calls it 'the imperial draft summarizing the council's purpose'. Which document each means was not settled. Kimel's note 33 names the author of the Westminster Handbook entry as Elizabeth Clark; Wikipedia's footnote names E. M. Harding with full details (Harding, E. M. (2004), pp. 162–167). Which is right was not settled.

other_findings.claim: PLACE BY PLACE, how secure is Origen's name? 400 synod (Theophilus) and Pope Anastasius: present and secure as to the name (named repeatedly; the texts survive in Jerome's correspondence, in one 13th-century manuscript). The Jerusalem bishops' reply (Ep. 93) anathematizes the listed propositions and whoever preaches them without naming Origen. 543 edict: present (Greek and Migne's Latin agree on 'Origen, who is also called Adamantius'); only Vincenzi denied the edict. 551 Confession of the Right Faith: securely absent. 553 Justinian's letter to the bishops: present (date disputed, 543 or spring 553). 553 fifteen anathemas: absent from every anathema and from the manuscript heading; Origen is in modern titles only. 553 session V: present in the Latin Acts (English only read here); challenged by Halloix and Vincenzi; what 'even now' refers to is disputed. 553 canon 11: present in the Latin Acts and in the Greek canons; no manuscript without it is reported; doubted on inference only. Vigilius 553-554: absent (the letter to Eutychius has no list of heresiarchs at all; Constitutum II not checked). Gregory the Great's letters on the councils: absent. Cyril c. 557 and Evagrius Scholasticus c. 593: present, in partisan or later narratives. Lateran 649, Trullo 692, Constantinople III 681 and Nicaea II 787: present, with Didymus and Evagrius.
other_findings.source: This cluster's passages; see each passage's sources.

other_findings.claim: NPNF's English of the 543 closing anathema ('Anathema to Origen and to that Adamantius') splits one person into two. The Greek τῷ καὶ Ἀδαμαντίῳ and Migne's Latin 'qui et Adamantius' both mean 'Origen, also called Adamantius'. Where the versions differ is in the rest of the sentence. NPNF cites Labbe and Cossart as its source, so the editor's note ('the Latin and Greek do not agree') may describe a printing I could not see.
other_findings.source: PG 86.1, cols. 989-990 (OGL OCR); NPNF II.14

other_findings.claim: Canon 11 of 553 differs from the Homologia's tenth anathema in more than Origen's name. It adds 'with their impious writings', the clause on heretics condemned by the four councils, and 'persisted in their impiety until death'. So canon 11 is a longer, reworked text. That fits Hefele's suggestion that the emperor or the bishops added Origen at the council, and it also fits an interpolator who started from the 551 list; the differences do not settle which.
other_findings.source: PG 86.1 col. 1017-1018 compared with DH 433 and the Greek text

other_findings.claim: The argument that Origen's last place in canon 11 is 'out of chronological order' is weakened by the Lateran list of 649, which is not chronological either (Paul of Samosata follows Severus and Theodosius). That shows such lists were not always compiled by date; it does not show that Origen's place in canon 11 is original. This is my own observation from the texts, not an argument I found in a scholar.
other_findings.source: DH 518-520 (clerus.org)

other_findings.claim: Vigilius's letter to Eutychius of 8 December 553 (in the NPNF translation) anathematizes Theodore of Mopsuestia 'together with all other heretics' condemned by the four councils and anathematizes no other heresiarch by name (Nestorius and Apollinaris are named only in descriptions of what Theodoret and Ibas wrote or defended). Its silence about Origen is therefore not a deliberate omission from a parallel list.
other_findings.source: NPNF II.14, 'The Decretal Letter of Pope Vigilius'

other_findings.claim: Theophilus's synodal letter of 400 lists among Origen's errors that 'the devil, freed from all the filth of sins, will be honoured equally and made subject together with Christ': an early charge touching the restoration of the devil, made against Origen's books. Rufinus preserves a letter in which Origen denies teaching it (not opened here).
other_findings.source: Jerome, Ep. 92.2.1, CSEL 55 p. 149 (OGL csel-dev)

other_findings.claim: Diekamp devotes a section (§ 7, from p. 67) to 'the transmission of the surviving Acts of the fifth general council and the genuineness of the two statements about Origen in them' (the fifth-session passage and canon 11). I could not read that section, so his conclusion is not reported here.
other_findings.source: Diekamp 1899, table of contents (archive.org OCR)

other_findings.claim: Misiarczyk observes that Evagrius of Pontus is not named in the Acts of 553, in Justinian's letter to the synod, or in the fifteen anathemas (nor, as Hefele suggests, in the 543 synod's letter to Menas), and that the first document to name him as a heretic is the Lateran synod of 649, canon 18.
other_findings.source: Misiarczyk, Vox Patrum 65 (2016), abstract and text

other_findings.claim: Kimel treats Origen's name in canon 11 as genuine ('Origen remains condemned in the eleventh canon', 2026, part 4) while saying it condemns him only 'generally'. In part 3 (n. 33) he notes the interpolation view as a minority view with current support, and separately (n. 3) he says he finds the hypothesis that the fifteen anathemas were interpolated into the Greek Acts 'attractive'.
other_findings.source: Kimel 2020; Kimel 2026 parts 3 and 4

other_findings.claim: In PG 86.1 (col. 989) the nine numbered anathemas of the 543 edict come first, and the ninth is the one on the end of punishment: 'If anyone says or holds that the punishment of demons and impious men is temporary ... that is, that there will be a restoration (ἀποκατάστασις) of demons or of impious men: let him be anathema.' The closing anathema against Origen, 'who set out these things', follows directly. The Latin beside it has 'restitutionem et redintegrationem' for the same word.
other_findings.source: PG 86.1, cols. 989-990 (OGL OCR, files 502.txt and 502.hocr), compared by the fact-checker

other_findings.claim: Straub's critical edition (ACO IV.1) has Origen's name in canon 11 in both languages, if Livorsi's quotations are right: Latin 'Origenem cum impiis eorum conscriptis' (218.8-9) and Greek 'καὶ Ὠριγένην μετὰ τῶν ἀσεβῶν αὐτῶν συγγραμμάτων' (242.32-33). Livorsi cites them in an article on another subject, so he gives no apparatus; I did not see the edition's notes on variants. Confirmed again on 2026-10-20 in Livorsi, n. 38 (p. 64), which sets 'εἴ τις μὴ ἀναθεματίζει Ἄρειον [...] καὶ Ὠριγένην' (ACO IV.1 242.32-33) beside 'si quis non anathematizat Arrium [...] Origenem cum impiis eorum conscriptis' (ACO IV.1 Can. XI 218.8-9).
other_findings.source: L. Livorsi, 'From Latin to Greek and Back Again', Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies 65 (2025), 48-79, n. 38 (read by the fact-checker)

other_findings.claim: Diekamp's table of contents has a section (§ 8, from p. 77) headed 'Die Zeugnisse für die Annahme, daß die fünfte allgemeine Synode nur über die drei Capitel verhandelt hat' (the testimonies for the view that the fifth general synod dealt only with the Three Chapters). I read the heading only, not his conclusion.
other_findings.source: Diekamp 1899, table of contents (archive.org OCR)

other_findings.claim: Jerome's Ep. 93, the Jerusalem bishops' reply to Theophilus's synodal letter, survives only in the same 13th-century manuscript as Ep. 92 and 95 (Ambrosianus H 59 sup.). It reports that some in Egypt wish to bring 'pestifera quaedam' into the churches on the strength of 'Origenis dogmatibus' and anathematizes anyone who preaches that Christ's kingdom will end or that the devil will regain his old dignity.
other_findings.source: Hilberg, CSEL 55, pp. 155-156 (OGL csel-dev XML, read by the fact-checker)

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, chronological order. For: Origen (died c. 254) comes after Eutyches (condemned 451) in a list otherwise in date order, which suggests the name was added (Ramelli 2019; Crouzel 1999; Schaff 1884 calls the connection 'incongruous'). Halloix's version, as Garnier reports it: some Acephalus put Origen in place of Dioscorus, who would have closed the list in order. Against: the list keeps the order in which each man was anathematized, and the council is 'only adding Origen last because he was not in the edict' (Truglia 2021); Origen, condemned in 543 or by the bishops just before the council, naturally comes last (Kimel comment 27 Dec 2021; Price 2009, vol. 2, p. 123 n. 86, as quoted by Baghos 2015).
other_findings.source: Ramelli 2019 (Brill PDF); Alura's translation of Crouzel 1999; Schaff HCC III §144; Garnier, PL 68.1075C; Truglia 2021; Kimel comment 27 Dec 2021; Baghos 2015 quoting Price

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, the 551 confession of faith. For: Justinian's 551 confession of faith against the Three Chapters (ὁμολογία; Latin 'Confessio rectae fidei') has a matching tenth anathema listing the same heretics without Origen (Hefele's reason c; Crouzel, whom Alura glosses as 'Homonoia/Confessio rectae fidei', number 10; Ramelli, who calls it the Homonoia; Harding, who calls the Homonoia the chancery's first draft of the anathemas). Against: Hefele says the emperor or the bishops may simply have gone further two years later. Truglia says a 551 document on the Three Chapters would not be expected to name Origen, and that expecting it is anachronism.
other_findings.source: Hefele, History of the Councils IV p. 336 (NPNF reprint); Truglia 2021; Ramelli 2019; Wikipedia 'Origenist crises' (Harding 2004)

other_findings.claim: UNSETTLED NAMING, 'Homonoia'. Ramelli (2019) calls the document whose list lacks Origen 'Justinian's Homonoia (Concord)'. Hefele calls it the emperor's 'omologia' (confession) and says its tenth anathema matches canon 11; Crouzel's 'corresponding list', no. 10, is glossed by Alura as 'Homonoia/Confessio rectae fidei'. Harding (via Wikipedia, citing her p. 166, note 20) calls the Homonoia 'the first draft of the anathemata issued by the imperial chancery'. Kimel (2026, part 3, n. 3) quotes McGuckin: 'a letter (homonoia) seems to have been issued by the emperor's personal cabinet to the assembled bishops'; Kimel elsewhere speaks of 'the original homonoia' as differing from the received canon. These may be one document or three. Hefele's and Crouzel's reading (the 551 Confession) is the only one for which I found the text: PG 86.1, col. 1017-1018, tenth anathema, which lacks Origen. If the Homonoia is instead a pre-conciliar draft of the 553 canons, the omission would be stronger evidence than the 551 parallel. An earlier note in this cluster called the name 'evidently a slip' for Homologia; that is too firm and has been withdrawn.
other_findings.source: Ramelli 2019; Hefele via NPNF; Kimel 2026 n. 3 and n. 33; Wikipedia 'Origenist crises'

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, Vigilius's documents. For: Vigilius's letter approving the council (to Eutychius, 8 Dec 553, Mansi 9:413–420) and his second Constitutum do not name Origen (Crouzel NCE; Ramelli 2019). Against: only the Three Chapters Acts were sent to the pope (Prat 1911); no copy of the anathemas sent to Vigilius survives (Truglia 2021); Vigilius is said to have signed Justinian's 543 edict naming Origen (Price, vol. 1, p. 43, as quoted by Truglia 2019). On one reading of Session V (the NPNF English), the council says Vigilius had condemned Origen 'now'.
other_findings.source: Encyclopedia.com (NCE, Crouzel); Ramelli 2019; Catholic Encyclopedia 1911 (Prat); Truglia 2019 and 2021

other_findings.claim: Check of REPORT.md (line 88: Origen is missing 'from the version Vigilius ...' signed). This is a fair report of E. M. Harding, but only as relayed by Wikipedia: 'nor does it appear in the version of the conciliar proceedings that was eventually signed by Pope Vigillius, a long time afterwards' (Harding 2004, p. 166). It should be attributed to Harding and marked as not checked against any manuscript or edition. What Crouzel and Ramelli say is narrower: Vigilius's own approving letters do not mention Origen. The Wikipedia article separately says the anti-Origenist open letter ratified by the bishops was not part of the official acts of the council; that is a different text from canon 11.
other_findings.source: Wikipedia 'Origenist crises' citing Harding 2004 p. 166; Encyclopedia.com (Crouzel); Ramelli 2019; REPORT.md line 88 and claims.md row 38

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, manuscripts and the Latin Acts. The original Greek text of the Acts is lost (Ramelli 2019); the Acts survive in an old Latin version (Straub's critical edition, Price's translation, per Wikipedia). The Roman archive copy, 'probably prepared for Vigilius himself', has Origen's name (Hefele). No known manuscript lacks it (Alura 2021). Harding (via Wikipedia) says the name is missing from the version of the proceedings Vigilius signed, but cites no manuscript. Tanner's edition, often cited for omitting the fifteen anathemas, prints Origen in canon 11. So far as anything read shows, the interpolation case rests on internal arguments.
other_findings.source: Ramelli 2019; Wikipedia 'Second Council of Constantinople'; Hefele via NPNF; Alura comment 26 Dec 2021; Tanner via papalencyclicals.net; Wikipedia 'Origenist crises' (Harding)

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, suspicion of tampering at Constantinople III (680–81). Ramelli says that 'suspicions have been raised already in 680 CE (at the Third Ecumenical Council of Constantinople) that the original Greek acts of the 553 CE council were interpolated'. The documents that council declared forged were the Logos of Patriarch Menas and two letters of Vigilius, which monotheletes used as proof texts. Ohme (2022), in his abstract, argues that these texts are authentic and describes a longer first edition of the Acts on papyrus rolls and a shorter second edition in codices. Wikipedia's article on the council says the alleged tampering is 'probably' false (citing Hefele). Nothing in the 680 dispute concerned Origen's name.
other_findings.source: Ramelli 2019; H. Ohme, 'Textkritik im Dienste der Wahrheitsfindung? Das VI. Ökumenische Konzil (680/81) und seine Fälschungsnachweise', Byzantinische Zeitschrift (2022), DOI 10.1515/bz-2022-0010, abstract (volume and pages not confirmed); Wikipedia 'Second Council of Constantinople' citing Hefele, Conciliengeschichte II, pp. 855–858

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, Theodore Ascidas. For (Halloix, Vincenzi, Hefele's reason a): Ascidas, an influential Origenist, would have prevented a condemnation of Origen. Against: Hefele says Ascidas had already anathematized Origen and would do so again if the emperor wished. Price doubts that Ascidas was an Origenist at all (vol. 1, p. 19 n. 40, pointing to vol. 2, pp. 273–4). Schaff (1884) says 'Perhaps also Theodore Askidas ... prevented the ecumenical condemnation of Origen. But this is a disputed point', and that no separate trial was necessary 'since a local synod of 544 had already condemned it'.
other_findings.source: Hefele via NPNF (tertullian.org); Price 2009 vol. 1 PDF p. 19; Schaff HCC III §144

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, ancient readers. Cyril of Scythopolis (Life of Sabas, written by about 558 at the latest per Truglia 2019; chapter number 90 not confirmed in the sources read; as translated by Price, vol. 2, p. 270): at the fifth council 'a common and universal anathema was directed against Origen and Theodore of Mopsuestia and against the teaching of Evagrius and Didymus on pre-existence and a universal restoration'. Evagrius Scholasticus (HE IV.38, c. 593; Walford 1846): the synod replied to Justinian 'after they had uttered exclamations against Origen'. Interpolationists answer that Cyril is a partisan anti-Origenist (Hombergen, per REPORT.md; not checked) and that Evagrius confused the pre-conciliar synod with the council (Whitby, as reported by Kimel 2020; Hombergen is reported there as saying Evagrius drew on 'existing contradictory traditions' about the council). Neither writer quotes canon 11.
other_findings.source: Truglia 2019 quoting Price; tertullian.org (Walford trans.); Kimel 2020

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, later councils. Trullo (692), canon 1: the 165 fathers under Justinian 'synodically anathematized and execrated Theodore of Mopsuestia … and Origen, and Didymus, and Evagrius'. Constantinople III and Nicaea II describe the fifth council the same way. The twelfth-century canonist Aristenus says the fifth council was held 'against the crazy Origen, Evagrius and Didymus', who taught 'an end of punishment'. Misiarczyk (2016) argues, for Evagrius's name, that these councils 'simply repeat the condemnation of the previous endemic synod without examining the case'. The same answer is available for Origen.
other_findings.source: NPNF II.14, Trullo canon 1 with Aristenus's note (CCEL); Misiarczyk, Vox Patrum 65 (2016), abstract (DOAJ)

other_findings.claim: A parallel case at the same council: Misiarczyk (2016) argues that 'the name of Evagrius does not appear' in the documents of 553 (the council, Justinian's letter to the synod about Origen, the edict against Origen), and that Evagrius was 'condemned probably only by some endemic synod before the official opening'. His name reached the record through the later councils. This is the closest analogue found to the 'name added' claim. It concerns the later councils' summaries, not the 553 text.
other_findings.source: Misiarczyk, 'Czy Ewagriusz z Pontu został rzeczywiście potępiony?', Vox Patrum 65 (July 2016), DOI 10.31743/vp.3510, English abstract (DOAJ); pages not stated

other_findings.claim: Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century line-up, per Diekamp: Cave, Dupin, Lequien and Walch thought Halloix's explanation 'essentially justified or at least probable'. Valesius and Jacques Basnage started the mediating view. Hefele and Schaff, however, list 'Basnage' with Halloix, so the Basnages (Samuel and Jacques) are reported inconsistently.
other_findings.source: Diekamp 1899, Einleitung (archive.org OCR); Hefele via NPNF; Schaff HCC III §144

other_findings.claim: Popular version 1, 'the name was added long after the council'. Hart ('Saint Origen', First Things, 1 October 2015): 'it was only well after the Fifth Ecumenical Council's close that they were attached to its canons, and Origen's name inserted into its list of condemned heretics.' Hart's review of Behr's On First Principles (Project MUSE article 757668, journal not identified) is also said to call the name's presence on the list 'again probably illegitimate'; this could not be re-checked because Project MUSE returned a verification page, so it rests on a search snippet that could not be re-opened. How it stands: no manuscript or ancient witness lacking the name is reported. The scholarly proponents (Ramelli, Harding) offer it as a likelihood from internal evidence. Kimel calls it a minority view. Hart's 'well after the close' has no documentary support in anything checked.
other_findings.source: firstthings.com/saint-origen; muse.jhu.edu/article/757668; Kimel 2026 n. 33

other_findings.claim: Popular version 2, 'Tanner's critical edition removes it'. Hart (2015) writes that Tanner 'simply omits the anathemas as spurious interpolations'. Tanner's own words are that the anathemas against Origen 'cannot be attributed to this council'. That refers to the fifteen, which Tanner calls neither spurious nor interpolated. Tanner prints canon 11 with 'and Origen'.
other_findings.source: papalencyclicals.net (Tanner's introduction and translation); firstthings.com

other_findings.claim: Popular version 3, 'Origen was never really condemned' (e.g., an OrthodoxWiki talk-page contributor in 2007: 'significant evidence that Origen's name is a later addition'). How it stands: even if the name in canon 11 were removed, Origen was condemned by Theophilus's synod (400), by Pope Anastasius, and in Justinian's 543 edict (which Price, as quoted by Truglia, says Vigilius signed). These earlier condemnations were not re-checked here. The only open question is whether an ecumenical council condemned him, and on what doctrines.
other_findings.source: orthodoxwiki.org/Talk:Origen; NPNF II.14 (543 anathemas); REPORT.md sections 2–3

other_findings.claim: Popular version 4, 'the pope never approved; he was Justinian's prisoner'. This is common in reincarnation literature, e.g. Head and Cranston, Reincarnation: The Phoenix Fire Mystery (1977), as quoted in a 2018 Medium post (the post was not re-opened in this check). That source also claims that the council's decrees were 'not accepted by Vigilius' successors' (quoting Britannica). How it stands: Vigilius refused to attend, but approved the council's decisions on the Three Chapters on 8 Dec 553 and 23 Feb 554 (Prat 1911). No papal document approves the fifteen anathemas, and Prat finds 'no proof' the pope's approval of them was asked. Vigilius is said to have signed the 543 edict naming Origen (Price, as quoted by Truglia 2019). The claim about the successors was not checked here; Pelagius I and later popes are usually said to have accepted the council (status R for that).
other_findings.source: graham-pemberton.medium.com (2018); Catholic Encyclopedia 1911 (Prat); Truglia 2019 citing Price vol. 1 p. 43

other_findings.claim: Twentieth-century specialists on the fifteen anathemas (Guillaumont 1962; Daley 1976 and 1991; Grillmeier) are cited in the sources checked for the target and date of those anathemas, not for the name in canon 11. No statement by any of them on the canon 11 interpolation question was found.
other_findings.source: fr.wikipedia 'Origénisme' (Daley 1976 p. 337); Kimel 2020 (Grillmeier); Encyclopedia.com (Crouzel on Guillaumont)

other_findings.claim: DISTINCT CLAIM, the fifteen anathemas were added later. Kimel (2020) reports that McGuckin proposed that the fifteen anathemas against Origen were 'quietly added to the synodal acts at a later date', and that Kimel himself does not argue that canon 11 is an interpolation. Hefele, Diekamp, Prat and Tanner treat the fifteen as pre-conciliar or not the council's. This is a different question from whether Origen's name in canon 11 was inserted, and popular writing (Hart 2015) often runs the two together.
other_findings.source: Kimel, 'Did the Fifth Ecumenical Council Condemn Universal Salvation?', Eclectic Orthodoxy (31 May 2020); Tanner via papalencyclicals.net; Prat 1911; Diekamp 1899 as reported by Kimel

other_findings.claim: Garnier's later revision: Diekamp notes that Garnier's dissertation on the fifth council was revised and reprinted (Hardouin's Theodoret Auctarium, Paris 1684; later in Schulze's edition, Halle 1774). other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, the principle of the list (the interpolation side's strongest form). For: the six names before Origen are the heretics the four earlier councils condemned, and they fall in the order of those councils (Arius, Nicaea; Eunomius and Macedonius, Constantinople I; Apollinaris, normally placed there; Nestorius, Ephesus; Eutyches, Chalcedon), and the canon adds 'all other heretics condemned ... by the Church and by the aforesaid four councils'. Origen was condemned by none of the four. Halloix's version (PL 68.1075C): the list is of heretics condemned in the four councils, so Origen was put in place of Dioscorus. Hefele lists it among the four reasons ('only such heretics would be named as had been condemned by one of the first four Ecumenical Synods') and calls them 'of insufficient strength, or mere conjecture'. Słomski (2025) gives the order version only. Against: Truglia and Kimel (2021) say the list keeps the order in which each man was anathematized, so Origen, condemned last, stands last; Price (via Baghos) says the last place reflects a real renewed condemnation of Origenism just before the council opened; the omnibus clause says 'by the Church', not only by the councils; the Lateran list of 649 is not in date order either. Gregory the Great's summary (next finding) fits the interpolation side's picture but omits Apollinaris, who is in canon 11. None of these answers shows the name was or was not original.
other_findings.source: Garnier PL 68.1075C via https://la.m.wikisource.org/wiki/Dissertatio_ad_Liberatum (read 2026-10-20); Hefele via https://tertullian.org/fathers2/NPNF2-14/Npnf2-14-114.htm (read 2026-10-20); Słomski p. 43; Truglia 2021; Baghos 2015 quoting Price

other_findings.claim: Gregory the Great, Epistle XXV (NPNF II.12, to John of Constantinople and the other patriarchs; the page gives no date): 'I confess that I receive and revere, as the four books of the Gospel so also the four Councils: to wit, the Nicene, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius is overthrown; the Constantinopolitan also, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius is refuted; further, the first Ephesine, in which the impiety of Nestorius is condemned; and the Chalcedonian, in which the pravity of Eutyches and Dioscorus is reprobated.' Of the fifth council he says: 'The fifth council also I equally venerate, in which the epistle which is called that of Ibas, full of error, is reprobated; Theodorus ... is convicted of having fallen into the perfidy of impiety; and the writings of Theodoritus ... are refuted'. Neither Origen nor Apollinaris is named on the page. No scholar I read ties this letter to canon 11; the parallel with the list is the interpolation advocate's own observation. His Latin and the Registrum number (NPNF's 'Book I, Epistle XXV'; the number in the Latin editions may differ) were not checked.

other_findings.claim: Hefele's four reasons and his replies, read at tertullian.org on 2026-10-20 (Hist. Councils IV, p. 336, in NPNF II.14, note on Capitulum XI): (a) Theodore Ascidas, 'the Origenist, was one of the most influential members of the Synod'; (b) 'only such heretics would be named as had been condemned by one of the first four Ecumenical Synods'; (c) the anathema 'is identical with the tenth in the omologia of the Emperor', where Origen's name is lacking; (d) Origen's errors differ from those of the group. Replies: 'insufficient strength, or mere conjecture'; the emperor may have 'subsequently went further than in his omologia', or the bishops 'of their own accord, added Origen'; the Roman copy of the Acts was 'probably prepared for Vigilius himself'; the New Lavra monks' break with the signing bishops, and 'the widely-circulated ancient rumour', are explained only if the name stood in canon 11. The advocates' charge that the REPORT leaves out Hefele's own concession that the name is absent from the emperor's 551 text is correct: on his second alternative, the name is an addition by the bishops at the council.

other_findings.claim: Kimel, 'Apokatastasis, Origen, and the Fifth Ecumenical Council (Part 3)', 9 Jan 2026, as read on 2026-10-20: n. 33, 'This minority view continues to find support among contemporary Church historians' (of the interpolation of Origen's name); n. 3, McGuckin: 'a letter (homonoia) seems to have been issued by the emperor's personal cabinet to the assembled bishops'; n. 16, Whitby: the anti-Origenist proceedings 'preceded the Council and were not regarded as a formal part of proceedings'; n. 10, Hombergen (p. 293): Cyril's 'representation of the facts . . . seriously contradicts the historical evidence'; and in the main text, Price (as Kimel gives it): 'the Latin translation was likely produced soon after the finalization of the Greek text'. The words are Kimel's quotations of others; Whitby, Hombergen, McGuckin and Price are therefore S, Kimel V.

other_findings.claim: State of the Acts, read 2026-10-20. Livorsi, GRBS 65 (2025): 'except for a few documents, the Acts of Constantinople are solely available in a Latin translation' (p. 59); the translation was 'made in the immediate aftermath of the council' (p. 60); the canons are among the few parts that survive in Greek (p. 63, nn. 35-37); the Latin is 'extremely literal' (p. 64). NPNF excursus: 'Between the Roman Manuscript printed by Labbe and the Paris manuscript found in Mansi there are considerable variations', and some of the most damaging material about Vigilius appears only in the Paris manuscript; after the sixth council's inquiry, 'the substantial accuracy of the rest of the acts have been established by the authority of the Sixth Synod'. The excursus does not say that the Greek original is lost (Ramelli does) and names no author on the page. Ohme (2022, abstract only) reports two editions of the Acts. What no source says: whether the Roman and Paris recensions, or the two editions, differ at canon 11. Livorsi names no manuscript of the Constantinople II Acts.

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, the cost of the hypothesis. For the name: to drop it one must also reject, or explain away, canon 11, the session V passage (Halloix, Vincenzi), the 543 edict (Vincenzi), and the reports of Cyril and Evagrius; no ancient reader is known to have suspected the name; the case begins with Halloix in 1648, whose motive was to clear Origen (Diekamp: 'eine krasse Tendenzschrift'). McClymond (2015, p. 818 n. 10): the interpolation 'must have been added so quickly to the original text that no one recognized it as an interpolation', and he asks how Ramelli can see it when 'no one before her seems to have done so'. Answer: the claim is old (Halloix, Garnier, Basnage, Walch, Vincenzi, as Hefele, Schaff and Diekamp record), and Ramelli replies that it 'was certainly not discovered by me'; the hypothesis is of an early insertion, so its being unnoticed later is expected. Limit: Diekamp's and Harnack's remarks on Halloix and Vincenzi are judgments of motive, not refutations; and an insertion made before Cyril wrote (c. 557) leaves little room. The Catholic Dictionary, as the NPNF page cites it, calls Vincenzi's attack on the Acts 'unworthy of serious notice'.
other_findings.source: McClymond and Ramelli reply (passage ramelli-mcclymond); Diekamp (passage halloix-1648); https://tertullian.org/fathers2/NPNF2-14/Npnf2-14-110.htm

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, the bridge from the name to the council's intent. Percival (NPNF II.14, excursus): even if the fifteen anathemas were adopted at the home synod, 'by including his name among those of the heretics in the XIth Canon, it practically ratified and made its own the action of that Synod'. Justinian's covering letter asks the bishops to anathematize each chapter 'together with the impious Origen', so the target was never in doubt, as even Kimel concedes (2026, part 4, n. 8). Limits: Kimel and Oxenham distinguish condemning Origen 'generally' from condemning every doctrine he taught; Truglia withdrew his earlier claim that canon 11 explicitly cites the 543 anathemas; and this argument assumes the name is genuine.
other_findings.source: https://tertullian.org/fathers2/NPNF2-14/Npnf2-14-115.htm (read 2026-10-20); Kimel part 4 https://afkimel.wordpress.com/2026/01/12/apokatastasis-origen-and-the-fifth-ecumenical-council-part-4/

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, motive and timing. The interpolation side: a party that already claimed the council's authority for its anathema had the motive, and the same milieu attached the fifteen anathemas to the 'fifth synod' by heading; Ramelli reports that the Sabaites 'maintained that the council issued a definitive anathema against Origen'; McGuckin (2017, as Kimel reports) holds that the fifteen were interpolated into the Greek Acts. Hart states the thesis flatly and gives no evidence in that essay. The genuine-name side: Cyril's account is a partisan's (Hombergen, as Kimel quotes him), which cuts both ways, since the earliest report of a conciliar anathema is also a partisan's; the question of the fifteen anathemas is a different question from the name in canon 11, and popular writing (Hart 2015) often runs them together.
other_findings.source: Ramelli PDF (above); Kimel part 3 notes 3, 10, 33; Hart https://firstthings.com/saint-origen/

other_findings.claim: ARGUMENT, the monks' reaction and the 'ancient rumour'. Hefele reads the break of the New Lavra monks with the bishops who signed the Acts, and the old report that the council anathematized Origen, as explained only by the name in canon 11 (V, tertullian.org). A Wikipedia article on Eustochius of Jerusalem says that at a Jerusalem synod 'all the bishops of Palestine, except for Alexander of Abila, confirmed the Fifth Council's verdicts' and that in 555 Eustochius 'drove some sixty monks' from the New Lavra; that article cites nothing for either sentence (S). Against: the reports come from Cyril, whom Hombergen and Kimel judge partisan or compressing, and the reaction would also follow if the pre-conciliar anti-Origenist proceedings (Whitby) were attributed to the council.
other_findings.source: https://tertullian.org/fathers2/NPNF2-14/Npnf2-14-114.htm; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eustochius_of_Jerusalem (read 2026-10-20)

other_findings.claim: WEIGHT OF SCHOLARSHIP. Diekamp (1899, Einleitung): by far most scholars of his day held Hefele's view that the council named Origen expressly, 'in passing and in a heap' (V, from the archive.org scan). Kimel (2026, part 3, n. 33) calls interpolation a 'minority view' that 'continues to find support among contemporary Church historians' (V). Alura (2021) calls it 'serious and respectable' and 'a reasonable conclusion', with 'no smoking gun' (V). Hold the name genuine: Hefele, Percival, Diekamp's majority, Crouzel (who accepts the name), Price, McClymond, Truglia, Kimel. Hold it inserted or possibly inserted: Halloix, Garnier (as reported), Basnage, Walch, Vincenzi, Ramelli, Harding (via Wikipedia), Hart, Słomski. No survey of present specialist opinion was found, so how the balance stands today is not known.
other_findings.source: Diekamp via archive.org item dieorigenistisch00diek; Kimel part 3; Alura (shamelessorthodoxy.com)

other_findings.claim: Crouzel's position, clarified. In the New Catholic Encyclopedia he writes that 'in its discussions little attention was paid to Origen, except to put his name in the list of heretics condemned in canon 11', and that Origen was not mentioned in the emperor's opening discourse, 'the source of the council's anathemas'. In 1999 (Alura's translation) he notes the name's last place 'although the other names are ranked by chronological order', asks 'What is the sense of this addition', and answers 'No' to whether Origen is condemned by the council as a matter of the canonical texts' own wording. So he accepts the name as present, records the anomaly, and doubts the condemnation's force and content. The REPORT's sentence that Crouzel 'argued that Origen was never properly condemned at all' reads as if he denied the name.
other_findings.source: https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/origen-and-origenism; https://shamelessorthodoxy.com/2021/01/21/orthodoxy-universal-salvation-are-the-two-compatible/

Method: the fetch tool returns quotations in fragments of under 125 characters, so long quotations were matched in segments; OCR corrections are listed in each passage's notes (Diekamp: 'dienten' read as 'Clienten', 'ovvodog ivdrjfxovoa' read as the Greek; Schaff on CCEL: 'as all interpolation' read as 'as an interpolation').
balance_note: Both sides are now heard on every passage where both exist. Canon 11 has the interpolation case (Halloix via Garnier, Słomski, Ramelli, Harding via Wikipedia, with Hart in the notes) and the genuineness case (Hefele with his four reasons and replies, Percival, Price via Baghos, Truglia, Kimel, Diekamp's majority), with Crouzel and Alura as the in-between readings. The 551 list and the Vigilius passage are split the same way; the fifteen anathemas hear Diekamp and Price, Hefele's 543 dating, Hart, Tanner, McGuckin's hypothesis (which concerns the fifteen, not the name) and Percival's undecided verdict; session V hears Percival and Truglia (genuine), Green and Price (genuine but an earlier act), Halloix and Vincenzi (forged). The two advocates agreed on almost every fact and differed on emphasis, so this merge did not have to choose between them on any point of evidence. Where they differed in what to call something, the account follows the sources: Homonoia is left unidentified; Vigilius's silence is split between 'no list to be missing from' and 'speaks as if he did not know'; the 680-81 inquiry is stated as it was; Crouzel is placed as a witness to the anomaly who accepts the name. Weak points that remain: no scholar of the interpolation side has examined the Latin manuscripts, and no scholar of the other side has either; Halloix, Vincenzi, Noris, the Ballerini and Harding are known only through reports; Diekamp's own chapter on genuineness could not be read; the modern defenders of interpolation (Ramelli, Harding, Słomski) rest on the internal evidence, and Hart gives none. The Vincenzi passage still has no modern defender of Vincenzi himself.
